prompt: Match each need to the service that answers it.
hint: Where does each one end?

pairs.left: the warehouse follows a live database within minutes
the database itself moves to Cloud SQL
a load once a night is enough

prompt: Why does a stream note the position in the source's log before it copies the first table?
hint: What happens to a change made while a table is being copied?

choices.text: So the copy can skip rows that will change
choices.why: Nothing is skipped; the copy reads what is there, and the changes are applied after it.

choices.text: So that no change made during the copy is lost
choices.why: Right: everything after that position is captured, so nothing falls between copied and captured.

choices.text: Because the log is deleted once the copy starts
choices.why: The log is kept, by the slot, until the reader confirms it.

choices.text: To lock the tables against writes during the copy
choices.why: Writes go on during the backfill; avoiding a lock is the point.

prompt: A stream is created with --backfill-none. What does it copy?
hint: Backfill is one half.

choices.text: The tables once, and no changes
choices.why: That is the opposite: no backfill means no copy of the tables.

choices.text: Nothing until a backfill is started by hand
choices.why: It streams changes from the moment it starts.

choices.text: Only the changes from the moment it starts
choices.why: Right: for tables already loaded some other way.

choices.text: The tables and the changes, more slowly
choices.why: That is --backfill-all, at the same speed.

prompt: Quitanda wants every past state of each order kept in BigQuery, not only the current one. Which destination setting fits?
hint: One mode writes every change as a new row.

choices.text: Merge mode with a short dataFreshness
choices.why: Merge keeps the current state of each row, however often it is refreshed.

choices.text: Append-only mode
choices.why: Right: every change becomes a row, and the history is a query.

choices.text: A Cloud Storage destination with Avro files rotated every 15 seconds
choices.why: Files would keep the changes, and the requirement is a BigQuery table.

choices.text: REPLICA IDENTITY DEFAULT on the source
choices.why: That decides how much of the old row the log carries, not how BigQuery stores the changes.

prompt: Which two names does a PostgreSQL source configuration for Datastream carry?
hint: The help printed them.

choices.text: A replication slot and a publication
choices.why: Right: replicationSlot and publication.

choices.text: A subscription and a trigger
choices.why: Datastream reads a slot; it neither subscribes nor installs triggers.

choices.text: The output plugin and the WAL segment size
choices.why: The plugin belongs to the slot, and the segment size to the server.

choices.text: A secret and a role
choices.why: The secret is the connection profile's, not the source configuration's.

prompt: What does the Datastream user on the shop's PostgreSQL need? Choose all that apply.
hint: It reads the log and the tables.

choices.text: The REPLICATION attribute
choices.why: Yes: to read the log through a slot.

choices.text: SELECT on the tables it copies
choices.why: Yes: for the backfill.

choices.text: INSERT on the tables, to mark what it read
choices.why: The slot remembers what was read; a CDC user that can write can change the history.

choices.text: Superuser, to create the slot during the stream
choices.why: The slot and the publication are created beforehand, and the stream names them.

prompt: The shop's database is in a rack, reached from Google Cloud over a VPN. Which connectivity does the section choose for the source profile, and why?
hint: Which options bring the database closer to the internet?

choices.text: Static IP connectivity, because it needs no VPC
choices.why: It works by admitting Google addresses through the database's firewall, which puts it closer to the internet.

choices.text: An SSH bastion, because it is the quickest to set up
choices.why: Quick, and a host facing the internet in front of the shop's database.

choices.text: A private connection peered with a VPC that reaches the rack
choices.why: Right: the database stays off the internet, and the VPN does the rest.

choices.text: None: Datastream reaches 198.51.100.20 directly
choices.why: That address is in a rack with no reason to be on the internet; something has to carry the path.

prompt: For a PostgreSQL server to write enough to its log for change data capture, `wal_level` must be ___.
hint: SHOW wal_level printed it.

prompt: The text slot was read with get, then read again with get at once. What did the second read return, and why?
hint: peek and get differ in one thing.

choices.text: The same nine rows, because get never moves the bookmark
choices.why: That is peek; get moves the bookmark past what it returned.

choices.text: An error, because the slot was dropped
choices.why: The slot still existed; it simply had nothing new.

choices.text: Zero rows, because get had moved the bookmark
choices.why: Right: once a reader takes its changes, the server forgets them for that slot.

choices.text: Only the commits, because the rows had been applied
choices.why: Nothing is applied by reading a slot; it returned nothing at all.

prompt: Match each first byte of a pgoutput message to what it is.
hint: One of them describes the table, once.

prompt: With the default replica identity, what does the log carry for a deleted order?
hint: Read the DELETE line of the text slot.

choices.text: The whole row as it was
choices.why: That needs REPLICA IDENTITY FULL.

choices.text: Only the primary key
choices.why: Right: order_id, which is enough to find and delete the row on the destination.

choices.text: Nothing: deletes are not logged
choices.why: The DELETE was there, with its transaction.

choices.text: The row number in the table file
choices.why: Logical decoding reports values, not physical positions.

prompt: A stream is paused for a long weekend on a busy source with no max_slot_wal_keep_size. What happens on the source?
hint: What does a slot keep, and for how long?

choices.text: The slot is dropped after an hour of inactivity
choices.why: No such timer exists by default; the slot waits for its reader.

choices.text: WAL piles up until the reader returns or the disk fills
choices.why: Right: the slot keeps everything its reader has not confirmed, without limit by default.

choices.text: Writes are refused until the stream resumes
choices.why: The source keeps writing; it is the log behind the writes that grows.

choices.text: Nothing, because Datastream reads the changes from BigQuery afterwards
choices.why: The changes exist only in the source's log until a reader takes them.

prompt: With max_slot_wal_keep_size at 32MB, the slot fell 71 MB behind and a checkpoint ran. What did the setting save, and what did it cost?
hint: Read wal_status before and after.

choices.text: It saved the stream and cost the disk
choices.why: The other way round: the log was removed, and the slot with it.

choices.text: It saved the disk and lost the slot
choices.why: Right: reading it is an error, and the way back is a new slot and a new backfill.

choices.text: It saved both, by compressing the old log
choices.why: Nothing was compressed; the segments past the limit were removed.

choices.text: Nothing, because 32MB only applies to new slots
choices.why: It applied to the existing slot at the next checkpoint.

prompt: In a continuous migration job, which command makes the Cloud SQL destination a standalone primary?
hint: The cutover has a name in DMS.

choices.text: migration-jobs stop
choices.why: Stopping pauses the replication; the destination stays a replica.

choices.text: migration-jobs verify
choices.why: Verify runs the job's checks and changes nothing.

choices.text: migration-jobs promote
choices.why: Right: promote ends the replication and makes the destination accept writes.

choices.text: migration-jobs demote-destination
choices.why: Demote goes the other way, turning an instance back into a destination of replication.

prompt: What does the pricing page say a PostgreSQL to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL migration costs in Database Migration Service itself?
hint: Same engine on both sides.

choices.text: $3.176 a GiB of changes in São Paulo
choices.why: That is the heterogeneous rate, for different engines.

choices.text: No additional charge, though the destination is billed
choices.why: Right: homogeneous migrations are offered at no additional charge, and Cloud SQL bills the instance.

choices.text: A flat fee per migration job
choices.why: The page has no per-job fee.

choices.text: An hourly rate for the replication instance
choices.why: There is no instance of yours to pay for in this service.

prompt: Put the cutover in the order that loses nothing.
hint: The writers stop before anything is promoted.
items: Run the job until it is quiet
Stop the writers on the source
Wait for the last changes and compare the counts
Promote the destination and point the applications at it
Drop the replication slot on the source

prompt: In São Paulo, Datastream CDC costs 3.176 USD a GiB for the first 2,500 GiB of a month. What do 80 GiB of processed changes cost, in USD, to two decimals?
hint: All of it is in the first tier.

prompt: The program printed 190.56 and 476.40 for the same month of Quitanda's changes. What does the lesson say to do with the two numbers?
hint: Where does the factor come from?

choices.text: Quote the average, 333.48, as the price
choices.why: An average of two guesses is a third guess; the factor is measurable.

choices.text: Run the stream for a week, read the processed bytes, then multiply
choices.why: Right: the factor depends on the data, and a week of the real stream measures it.

choices.text: Quote 190.56, since 2x is the page's usual case
choices.why: The page gives a range of two to five, not a usual case.

choices.text: Ignore both, because CDC under 2,500 GiB is free
choices.why: The first tier is $3.176 a GiB; only AlloyDB and Spanner sources have 100 GiB free.

prompt: A month after the cutover, the old shop database is running out of disk although nobody writes to it any more. What is the likely cause?
hint: What was left behind?

choices.text: The backfill is still copying the tables
choices.why: The backfill ended long before the cutover.

choices.text: A replication slot that nobody reads, still holding WAL
choices.why: Right: the sixth step of the cutover, dropping the slot, was skipped.

choices.text: The publication duplicates every row it names
choices.why: A publication only names tables; it stores nothing.

choices.text: REPLICA IDENTITY FULL on a read-only table
choices.why: It adds to updates and deletes, and a read-only table makes neither.

prompt: Which of these are true of the two slots in the practice? Choose all that apply.
hint: Same log, two bookmarks.

choices.text: Each saw the same three transactions
choices.why: Yes: the same xids, 733 to 735, as text in one and binary in the other.

choices.text: Reading one with get left the other's changes in place
choices.why: Yes: each slot has its own bookmark.

choices.text: The pgoutput slot reported ord-1's first insert
choices.why: ord-1 was inserted before either slot existed, so neither reports it.

choices.text: Both held the same retained size after the bulk insert
choices.why: Yes: 3431 kB each, since neither had been read past the bulk insert.

prompt: Why does Datastream's source configuration need a publication when its slot already exists?
hint: What does pgoutput publish?

choices.text: pgoutput publishes only the tables the publication names
choices.why: Right: the slot is the bookmark, and the publication is the list of tables.

choices.text: The publication stores the changes until Datastream reads them
choices.why: The slot keeps the log; a publication stores nothing.

choices.text: It sets wal_level to logical
choices.why: wal_level is a server setting, set when the server starts.

choices.text: It gives the user the REPLICATION attribute
choices.why: That is granted to the role, with ALTER ROLE.
